Nuts
nŭts
n. pl. (hard-shelled fruits; part of Jacob's present and the garden of the Song)
From Old English hnutu. Two different Hebrew words are rendered nuts: botnim in Genesis 43:11, pistachios, and egoz in the Song, the walnut — both prized and both grown in the land, not in Egypt.

Biblical Definition

Israel, forced to send Benjamin into Egypt, sends a present with him and chooses it carefully: “And their father Israel said unto them, If it must be so now, do this; take of the best fruits in the land in your vessels, and carry down the man a present, a little balm, and a little honey, spices, and myrrh, nuts, and almonds” (Genesis 43:11). Every item is a specialty of Canaan and none of them is a staple — there is a famine on, and a starving family is sending delicacies. The gift is an old man's courtesy under duress, and it is aimed, without his knowing it, at the son he thinks is dead. The other appearance is in the Song, where the beloved walks out to see whether anything is growing: “I went down into the garden of nuts to see the fruits of the valley, and to see whether the vine flourished, and the pomegranates budded” (Song of Solomon 6:11). Walnut groves, vines, and pomegranates belong to the vocabulary of a land at rest, the opposite of Genesis 43's famine. Scripture's catalogue of the good land is specific about its produce, and the specificity is part of the doctrine: the covenant God gives a real country with real trees in it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a nut as the fruit of certain trees and shrubs, consisting of a kernel covered by a hard shell.

expand to see more

NUT, n. [Sax. hnut.] The fruit of certain trees and shrubs, consisting of a hard shell inclosing a kernel.

NUT, n. In mechanics, a small cylinder or other body, with teeth or wings; the small piece of metal with a screw cut in it, which is screwed on the end of a bolt.

ALMOND, n. [Fr. amande.] The fruit of the almond tree; a nut containing a kernel.

BALM, n. [L. balsamum.] The sap or juice of trees or shrubs remarkably odoriferous or aromatic.

PRESENT, n. That which is presented or given; a gift; a donative.

Key Scripture

Genesis 43:11 — "And their father Israel said unto them, If it must be so now, do this; take of the best fruits in the land in your vessels, and carry down the man a present, a little balm, and a little honey, spices, and myrrh, nuts, and almonds:"

Song of Solomon 6:11 — "I went down into the garden of nuts to see the fruits of the valley, and to see whether the vine flourished, and the pomegranates budded."

Jeremiah 17:11 — "As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool."

Proverbs 6:8 — "Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest."

Modern Corruption

Scripture's attention to ordinary produce is treated as incidental colour, and the goodness of created, edible, particular things is quietly spiritualized away.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift is a kind of piety that finds the material embarrassing. Genesis pauses in the middle of a famine narrative to name balm, honey, spices, myrrh, nuts, and almonds, and a reader trained to look only for doctrine skips the list. The principle to recover is that God made a world with pistachios in it and put the inventory in His book. Gnosticism has never stopped being the church's most persistent unacknowledged heresy, and it always begins by finding the physical beneath notice.

There is also a small pastoral lesson in Jacob's present. He is frightened, he has lost one son and is being made to risk another, and what he does is send a gift of the best his land can still produce. It changes nothing about the danger. It is the gesture of a man doing the one courteous thing left within his power while the outcome rests entirely elsewhere — and the reader, who knows who is waiting in Egypt, watches an old man's small kindness travel toward the son he is mourning.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew botnim (H992), pistachio nuts; egoz (H93), a walnut; shaqed (H8247), an almond; tsori (H6875), balm.

expand to see more

Hebrew botnim (H992) — pistachios; only Genesis 43:11, among Jacob's present.

Hebrew egoz (H93) — a walnut; only Song of Solomon 6:11, the garden of nuts.

Hebrew shaqed (H8247) — an almond, the waker; Jeremiah 1:11, the rod of an almond tree.

Hebrew tsori (H6875) — balm; the balm of Gilead, Jeremiah 8:22.

Hebrew zimrath ha-arets (H2173) — the best fruits of the land; Jacob's phrase for the gift.

Usage

"“Nuts, and almonds” — delicacies sent out of a famine."

"“The best fruits in the land” — and every item grows in Canaan."

"“The garden of nuts” — the vocabulary of a land at rest."
